articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Not Tell Someone You’re Sick Before You Meet Up?
articles.content:
“Mom? My throat feels like I swallowed razor blades, doused them in gasoline and lit them on fire.” Then my dramatic child did what children do and coughed right in my face. It was one week before we were set to fly for a much-anticipated vacation in another state to visit family members we hadn’t seen in forever. As soon as I felt the droplets hit my face, I knew we were all doomed—her, me, the rest of the family, the folks we were visiting and maybe some of the general public.
I probably should have seen it coming. It was the first week of school, and back-to-school might as well be called back-to-flu. And sure enough, two days later, my throat also felt like I swallowed razor blades, doused them in gasoline and set them on fire. (She may have been dramatic, but she wasn’t wrong.) I did, however, manage to refrain from coughing in anyone’s face.
What should we do?
Cold and flu season creates an etiquette dilemma because getting sick isn’t a social offense or a moral failing. It’s just human. And sometimes you don’t know you’re sick until you’re already standing in someone else’s kitchen. Or you attribute feeling a little fatigued or sniffly to just being, well, a little fatigued. It literally could be nothing. That being said, there’s a big a difference between coming down with the sniffles mid-event and knowingly showing up to a four-hour indoor party while hacking up a lung like consumption is in vogue again.
So what is the polite thing to do if you feel like you’re coming down with something or you’re flat-out sick? Is it really rude to not tell someone you’re sick before you meet up? Grab a box of tissues, and let’s discuss.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Telling people you’re sick is simply about giving them the information they need to make the decision that’s best for them. Your infectious status is important info for regular healthy people, but it’s even more important for people who really need to avoid getting sick, like people who are pregnant, very old, very young or immunocompromised. Not telling them could have terrible consequences. It is also very pertinent info for people who may be preparing for an important event like a wedding, vacation or surgery. And you likely don’t know all of those circumstances because people don’t usually preemptively announce what they can’t get sick for.
There’s a practical reason to share as well: You probably look sick. If you show up with two pockets stuffed full of tissues and a voice like Al Pacino, they’re going to know something is up. Realizing that you knew you were sick and didn’t say anything may feel like a frustration, at best, and a betrayal, at worst.
Of course, we do need to mention the friend who’s a germophobe (and you privately think is being a little ridiculous). There’s a definite temptation not to tell them because they’ll turn it into A Big Thing, but I’d say that’s even more of a reason to let them know. Anxiety often stems from a lack of information. You being matter-of-fact and honest can help allay their fears. Or they’ll cancel, but that’s their decision to make.
The important distinction here is that telling someone you’re sick isn’t the same as asking for permission. You can say, “Hey, I woke up with a head cold, and I just wanted to let you know before we met up. Totally get it if you’d rather reschedule.” Boom, done. Now they have the information, and they can decide what they feel good about doing.
There are also good reasons for not turning every sneeze into an emergency alert. Sometimes, extra information just causes extra stress, especially for people already prone to worrying about getting sick. Colds are endemic. Telling someone you have a little cold during cold season isn’t particularly surprising or unique. After all, nearly everyone is sniffling then, and they’ll be sniffling and sneezing all around you when you’re out.
Not to mention that people don’t always know when they’re contagious. You can wake up feeling completely normal, go through your day and realize at night that you have a sore throat. Maybe your sniffly nose is just allergies. Or you have a lingering cough from a cold three weeks ago that’s no longer contagious. And we’ve all had those days when we feel more tired than usual and wonder if it’s the onset of an illness or just too many churros while binge-watching The Pitt. (That last one might just be me.) At any rate, expecting someone to diagnose themselves correctly before every social occasion is a pretty high bar.
And do others really need that info about you? Privacy is a swiftly dwindling resource these days, and we should hold on to the few shreds we have left, even if those shreds are in our sinuses. Plus, for people who tend to disclose too much, feeling like you need to report all your symptoms can be a terrible type of oversharing—especially if it involves anything below the waist. People don’t want or need the play-by-play of your bathroom adventures.
Of course, the best etiquette advice about whether or not to tell someone you’re sick before you meet up is … it depends. On what?
One gray area that isn’t so gray: the idea that you already committed, so you have to go, no matter what. People sometimes feel that canceling is worse than showing up sick because “I said I’d be there.” But most hosts would rather avoid germ exposure or at least be given a heads-up about it.
Just keep it simple. They don’t need to send a medical dissertation. Something like: “Just a heads-up that I woke up with a cold today. I’m feeling OK, but I wanted you to know before we got together. Totally understand if you’d rather reschedule.”
Or if you’re not sure whether you’re actually sick: “I have a scratchy throat today, and I’m not sure if I’m coming down with something. I feel fine otherwise, but I wanted to give you a heads-up.”
Or if you know you’re genuinely sick: “Hey, friend. I’m definitely sick, so I think we should reschedule. I’m sorry. I was really looking forward to seeing you.”
Notice that all three messages avoid pressuring the other person. You’re also not saying that it’s not a big deal and the other person shouldn’t worry about it. Give them the information, and let them decide.
Time to make your own personal-risk calculation. Of course, that will look different for each person. If you’re uncomfortable for any reason, it’s perfectly fine to ask to change plans—like moving things outside—or excuse yourself. No need to make a dramatic announcement or accuse them of being irresponsible.
“I’m actually trying really hard not to get sick right now. Would you mind if we reschedule?” is great.
Canceling the trip didn’t feel like an option—the visit was too important. Neither my daughter nor I had a particularly serious illness (we tested negative for both COVID and the flu), and no one involved was elderly or immunocompromised. But my husband and I agreed that we needed to tell our family before we showed up. They weren’t thrilled, but they still wanted us to come. So we wore masks on the airplane and in common areas, stayed in a hotel instead of their house and changed several of our activities to be outdoors.
And you know what? The trip turned out great. Everyone had a wonderful time, in large part because nobody was surprised when we showed up sick.
Yes, it’s rude not to tell someone you’re sick before you meet up … if your illness could reasonably change whether someone wants to see you. Not every circumstance will require a disclosure, but as a general rule of thumb, this is information that’s polite to share. If they opt to reschedule, don’t take it personally. But if they want to see you anyway, do your best to minimize germ exposure. And if you know you’re sick sick—or you’re going to be around people who are especially vulnerable—consider canceling or changing the plans rather than putting others in the uncomfortable position of deciding for you.
The etiquette isn’t about whether you got sick; it’s about giving people enough information to decide whether they want to spend the afternoon with you and whatever microscopic hitchhikers you’ve brought along.
As for my daughter’s razor-blades-on-fire throat? We both recovered, our family survived the trip, and nobody else got sick. Which proves that sometimes a little honesty, a few precautions and a healthy respect for other people’s lungs can go a long way. Although I still maintain that “my throat feels like I swallowed razor blades and lit them on fire” was an unnecessarily elaborate way to ask for a popsicle.

articles.title: We Tried a Beginner’s Pottery Kit—And Now We Wanna Clay All Day
articles.content:
Time away from screens is absolutely essential, especially in the age of AI. That’s why the recent rise of analog hobbies has been nothing short of a miracle for my mental health. In fact, spending a few minutes with a mini coloring book or investing in a monthly book subscription is an easy way to boost dopamine during my downtime—no doomscrolling required.
But the best hobbies are those that require practice and patience. That’s where at-home pottery kit brand Pottd comes in. These clever at-home pottery kits come with almost everything you need to put together pots, paint mugs or make your bestie an incense burner. And the best part? You don’t need any experience with clay to craft cute pieces. Here’s my experience getting hooked on these all-inclusive kits.
Pinch pots, painted mugs and pressed clay coasters—oh, my! Pottd kits come with dozens of different projects that scratch that creative itch.
There are several kits on Pottd to choose from, which fall into two categories: painting and pottery. Painting kits come with premade items along with the paints to decorate them. Pottd offers dozens of kits that come with things like picture frames, mugs, beer glasses, coasters or vases—you name it.
The pottery kits bring additional choices. Pick from general creativity kits or opt for specific kits that cover things like biscuit-shaped coasters, candle holders, baby keepsakes, sculptural plants, games and more. There are also extras like molds and paints available à la carte.
I opted for a general kit with “retro” paint colors. Pack neatly inside the kit is nearly everything you’ll need to make several different pieces, including:
First, take everything out of the box and arrange it on a flat surface. Now is the perfect time to unfurl that junk mail or those local grocery mailers crowding in your mailbox—they make excellent protection for your table!
The Quick Start guide is a great resource when first setting up your pottery zone. It outlines any extras you might want that don’t come with your kit, such as additional tools. While I didn’t have a ruler or rolling pin on hand, I did take its advice to ensure I had a cup of water set up for smoothing and adding “slip” to the clay. I also grabbed a reusable paper towel to keep messes to a minimum.
Next, I highly recommend setting the mood. If you’re like me, that means adding some background noise and good, solid lighting. While you can absolutely make your pottery in silence, popping on a good podcast, audiobook, or your favorite album helps keep that creativity flowing.
The Quick Start guide also comes with several instruction cards covering projects like a trinket dish, pinch pot, incense burner, vase, draped dish, photo stand and plant pot. Reading through these cards is super helpful when you’re considering your first pieces!
For my first project, a pinch pot, I unpacked one of the clay packets and separated out 1/4 of the bag as instructed. The rest goes back into the sealed bag for future projects. I popped the instruction card into the cardboard holder and got started.
Overall, the instructions are detailed and perfect for newbies. They go over each step in an easy-to-follow format, leaving plenty of room for creative choices. I especially appreciated the continued reminders to use water and the included sponge to keep the clay surface nice and slick. This clay tends to crack when it’s dry, so keeping it moist while you work is crucial for a nice, smooth look.
After making my pinch pot, I caught the creativity bug and decided to crank out an incense burner and a draped dish. This time, I also had a clearer direction: I wanted to model them after my favorite noms—breakfast foods! Even after crafting a bacon-shaped incense burner, an egg-shaped dish and my little pinch pot, I still had about a third of my first bag of clay leftover. I didn’t even dip into my second bag, so each box can easily handle several projects.
The hardest part was waiting for the clay to dry, which took about 48 hours. After that, you must apply a base coat, which takes about 1-2 hours to dry. It’s important to ensure that pottery is completely dry before painting. Once dry, it was time to paint my pottery!
This is the fun part! Using the paints that come in the kit, it’s time to decorate your pottery. For the best results, Pottd recommends working in thin layers and waiting for each layer to dry before adding another. Now is the time to get creative with stripes, spots, murals or whatever inspires you.
I used a reference photo for my bacon incense burner, and I’m pretty pleased with how it turned out! While the kit didn’t come with a white paint for my egg whites, I opted for a baby blue color and think it turned out pretty darn cute. For my pot, I pursued a polka-dotted aesthetic.
Once the paint has dried completely, the final step is to give it a good glaze. This step is optional, but it gives the pottery a more finished look. Plus, the glaze protects the paint from scratches and adds slight water resistance, though it’s best to keep all pottery away from water for the best longevity. Skipping this step gives the pottery a more rustic look, should that be your preferred direction.
Once you begin making clay pieces from a Pottd kit, it’s quite an addictive hobby! I found myself thinking about my next project soon after finishing my first batch. And because each kit includes so much clay, I was able to make a few pieces to give to friends as gifts as well. Overall, Pottd kits are an easy way to try out a new hobby. I already have my eye on additional kits like the Paint a Tea Set kit and the overstuffed Super Bundle.
Pottd kits span tons of options, including pottery, picture holders and pretty tea sets!
Folks looking for an all-in-one kit that makes it easy to experiment will love how inclusive Pottd kits are. Plus, they make great gifts for creatives or date night activities for couples’ holidays like anniversaries and Valentine’s Day. The brand is always rolling out new kits and creative tools, so check out the Pottd website to see what’s currently trending!

articles.title: If You See Orange Flames on Your Gas Stove, This Is What It Means
articles.content:
Cooks have long loved the distinctive whoosh of firing up a gas stove. The flames pop up quickly and provide consistent heat, making it easy to cook with pinpoint control. Gas stoves also save the day if you need to cook when the power’s out because they don’t require electricity (for the cooking part, anyway). As a cook and an electrician, I wouldn’t give up mine for anything.
Unfortunately, gas stoves hide lurking dangers behind that satisfying flame. One major problem is air quality. We’ll dig into the specifics below, but in a recent study published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health, researchers found that nearly 13% of childhood asthma in the United States is caused directly by gas stoves. And that’s just one of the findings.
Even a perfectly functioning gas stove gives off invisible fumes. But keeping your eyes peeled for odd flame colors can help you diagnose major safety risks before they get out of hand. To find out more about gas stoves and safety, I spoke to Troy Legg, a virtual appliance technician with home-warranty company American Home Shield. He has more than 20 years of experience repairing appliances, including gas stoves, and knows exactly what color the flames should be.
Read on to find out what it means if you see different colors and what you should be doing to keep your gas stove in tip-top shape.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more safety, cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
“A healthy gas-burner flame is usually blue,” Legg says. There’s room for a tiny bit of variation, but not much. “With natural gas, a blue flame with a slight white tip can be normal,” Legg adds. “With liquid propane, a blue flame with a small yellow tip can also be normal.”
But if most of the flame, not just the tip, turns a different color, that’s a signal that something is wrong.
Blue flames indicate that complete combustion of natural gas is taking place. Natural gas is mostly methane, and when it burns correctly on your stove, all of the fuel gets used up and turned into heat, water vapor and carbon dioxide (CO2). The flames are blue because the light produced within this clean-burning flame has a short wavelength. (Remember the ROYGBIV of a rainbow? The red side has longer wavelengths, and the blue-indigo-violet side has shorter ones.)
Natural gas produces a very hot flame—as high as 3,500 degrees Fahrenheit. In contrast, wood fires burn cooler and less cleanly, giving off soot and wood particles. It’s these particles that produce the campfire-like orange and red flames you should never see on your gas cooktop.
“A steady yellow or orange flame can signal incomplete combustion, often caused by dirty burners, blocked openings or an improper gas-to-air mixture,” Legg says. Instead of methane converting to CO2 and water vapor, some of the gas is not used and is released into the air, which is not ideal.
But not all situations are reason to panic. “A small amount of white or yellow tipping can be normal depending on the type of gas and the appliance,” Legg says. Dust in the air can create brief yellow flickers, and he says calcium and other minerals may burn orange. “But a flame that is mostly yellow, orange or red should be checked by a professional.”
Because blue flames are the normal state of affairs, the sudden appearance of orange or yellow means your stove is trying to tell you something. Here’s why these flames can be a big problem.
“A steady yellow or orange flame may mean the burner is dirty or the gas and air are not mixing properly,” Legg says. Either one can “affect combustion and potentially create a carbon monoxide (CO) risk,” he says. According to the EPA, the air around a properly working gas stove contains about 5 to 15 parts per million (ppm) of CO, and a poorly adjusted one can have levels of 30 ppm or higher.
Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas that kills hundreds of people every year and sends 100,000 to the emergency room, according to the CDC. Children are particularly vulnerable, as are the elderly and people with breathing conditions. If you have a gas stove, putting in a CO monitor to alert you of high CO levels can be a lifesaver.
Orange flames are inefficient and will cost you money. In incomplete combustion, some of the gas coming out of your burners is flat-out wasted, so you have to use more gas to get the right amount of heat for cooking. That will translate into a higher gas bill over time.
Besides dangerous CO buildup, gas stoves are also known to contribute to poor indoor-air quality more generally (remember that asthma stat). Methane, nitrogen dioxide, benzene and other volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are released from even well-functioning stoves, and if your stove burns inefficiently, it gives off more of them.
This one’s not dangerous, but it could be disappointing if you’re hungry. Gas flames that are uneven or inefficiently burning, which often happens when you’re seeing those orange or yellow flames, can create hot spots, make you crank up the heat and otherwise decrease the quality of your cooking experience.
Legg says the main one to watch out for is red. “A red flame is less common and could point to an issue with gas quality, so homeowners should contact their gas provider if they see a persistent red flame,” he says. Gas-quality problems can include a range of issues, from an inconsistent delivery pressure to the presence of impurities that affect how the gas burns.
Another interesting twist involves the presence of a humidifier in your home. Humidifiers give off water vapor, of course, but that vapor also carries minerals like calcium and potassium. Legg mentioned calcium’s orange color earlier, but also be on the lookout for potassium’s pink or purple hue. Though these color changes are not dangerous, using distilled water will reduce these effects.
“Start with basic cleaning and inspection,” Legg says. “Make sure the burner cap is seated correctly, then check the burner openings for food, grease or debris.” Turn all knobs to the off position and remove the burner caps and heads. “A paper clip can be used gently to clear blocked burner holes and the small center orifice,” Legg says. Don’t use a wooden toothpick—it might break off, which could block the port and cause gas to back up.
You can also wash the parts of the burner assembly, but avoid soaking them. “Use a damp cloth instead of a soapy or wet cloth, since excess moisture can get into the spark switches and cause unwanted sparking,” Legg says. “After cleaning, make sure all parts are completely dry and properly reassembled before trying the burner again.”
“If the flame remains yellow, orange or red, or if there is any gas smell, stop using the appliance and contact a qualified repair technician or the gas provider,” Legg says. “An unusual flame color or smell can indicate a serious matter and potential safety risk. So if you notice something questionable, don’t wait to contact a professional or your gas provider.”

articles.title: Teens Are Getting Arrested After Posting a Dr. Seuss Meme—Here’s What’s Going On
articles.content:
At the risk of sounding old, it’s hard to keep up with what kids are doing online these days. Even uttering that sentence puts me firmly in the relic category, but … 6-7? Come on now! What are we even doing here?
The latest viral meme, involving a Dr. Seuss character who is definitely not teaching the youth their ABCs, seems silly and ridiculous at first glance—but is actually pretty terrifying. Sharing the meme has also had some very real, very scary consequences that you and your kids should be aware of.
I’ve been on the internet since the mid-1990s, so I have some big Gen X energy around online trends. My biggest fear was getting caught illegally downloading a few songs from Napster. (Which I barely did! I love copyright law!) But when I got a look at this creepy new meme, it had me wishing for the good old days.
To find out about this internet trend that’s increasingly getting the police called and has even led to some teen arrests, I spoke with Lt. Steven Orcutt with the Potter County Sheriff’s Department in Texas. Read on to learn what this viral trend is, why it’s a big deal and how to protect your children from consequences that could follow them around for life.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, tech, cleaning, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
@cnn Videos showing a person dressed up as Cat in the Hat roaming streets after dark have spread across social media, even prompting responses from police in Ireland and the UK. But it remains unclear which, if any, of the sightings are real or if they are AI-generated. #catinthehat ♬ original sound – CNN
It’s called the Cat in the Hat meme. “This current trend began as a dark-humor meme using clips from the 2003 Cat in the Hat movie,” says Orcutt. “It has since evolved into an AI-generated hoax trend, where users create realistic-looking images and videos of the Cat in the Hat lurking around homes, neighborhoods, schools and other public spaces.”
The posts started on Snapchat and were circulating in Ireland and the U.K. in August, according to the Guardian. From there, they made their way across the ocean and to multiple platforms, including TikTok and, to a lesser degree, Instagram. The posts can be accompanied by creepy music and even threatening messages.
“Many posts claim the character is ‘coming to’ a specific town, school or community in a way of inciting fear or making vague statements of harm,” Orcutt says. Case in point: “On my way to Kentucky next, be looking out,” read one Cat in the Hat message on TikTok. Sometimes the meme has a real-life element, and the character is filmed chasing actual people.
But no matter what form the meme takes, the idea is to sow fear and confusion. “While the trend is not tied to real-world violence, it creates several issues,” Orcutt says.
“In short, it’s an internet hoax,” Orcutt says, “but the reaction to it can create real-world problems.”
Yes, several. “This is a national social media hoax, and not a localized threat,” Orcutt says. Teens from all over the country have been caught up in the hype and aftermath.
A 14-year-old in Grand Junction, Colorado, was arrested after posting a version of the meme that referenced a threat to a middle school.
